source_locator.description: Opening action prose before the first labelled utterance.

translation.english_text: A coach arrives and stops. Baladevar, the queen and the others get down and go inside. Muthan, who drove the coach, also gets down. He takes the horse. A picture falls from it. Sukhadev notices.
notes: `அவன் குதிரையை எடுக்கிறான்` is kept conservatively as `He takes the horse`; no extra action such as tying or leading it away is added.

translation.english_text: Hey—Mutha! What picture is this?
Nothing...
Hey!... Just show me; let me see...

source_locator.description: Bracketed action immediately after Sukhadev asks to see the picture.

translation.english_text: [He shows it.]
Oh!... Mutha! I remember seeing a picture like this somewhere two or three weeks ago!...
What you are about to see... this picture is my dream of an ideal... the dawn-star of joy... The picture you saw a week or two ago was another copy of this picture—an unfinished drawing...
notes: The source's `லட்சியக் கனவு / இன்ப விடிவெள்ளி` image sequence is preserved rather than compressed into a plain description of the portrait.

translation.english_text: Oh-ho! Was that yours too?
Yes. The earlier one slipped from my hand and was stolen....! I drew another one. That... this...
All right; all right, Mutha. If there were a woman in this world like the one in this picture, I would be the one to marry her.
Hm; why talk about something that does not exist.
True enough—what people talk about in this world is what does not exist... All right, aren't you coming to the monastery?
Village meeting.
notes: The source is an abrupt two-word fragment, `ஊர் கூடம்.`; the English remains equally elliptical.

source_locator.description: Bracketed entrance cue after Muthan's `ஊர் கூடம்.` reply.

translation.english_text: [Muthan's friends arrive.]
What, Muthanna, all well?
notes: `முத்தண்ணா` is retained as `Muthanna`; `சுகந்தானா?` is rendered as the colloquial `all well?`.

translation.english_text: What, is this some land of freedom for us to live in comfort? The man of comfort is right inside this monastery—Maykainatha Swami.
notes: The verified Tamil prints `சுந்திர பூமி`; the English carries the evident freedom/comfort wordplay without altering that Tamil reading.
The second `சுக` image is retained as `man of comfort`, keeping the satirical wordplay before Maykainatha Swami is named.

translation.english_text: May Ammaiyappan's grace reach the entire universe... O servants of the servants! O devotees filled with love!....... If you have questions of doubt, ask and gain clarity........
notes: The devotional proclamation and extended pauses are preserved; `அய்ய வினைகள்` is translated by sense as questions of doubt without repairing the Tamil source.

translation.english_text: Swami, what does `Ammaiyappan` mean.........
notes: The title-name `Ammaiyappan` is retained because the following exchange turns on its Tamil `Amma/Appa` wordplay.

translation.english_text: Goodness, don't you understand even this, Prince? This palaiyakkarar Baladevar here is your...
notes: `பாளையக்கார` is retained as `palaiyakkarar`, a source-specific political/feudal title, rather than flattened to a generic `lord`.

translation.english_text: Father!......
Right, and she.......?
Mother!.......
Amma...... Appa...... Ammaiyappa.
notes: The Tamil mother/father wordplay is preserved by transliteration; replacing it with a fully English compound would erase the title's sound-play.

translation.english_text: Oh! Then is it my mother and father whose hides you are wearing!
notes: The source's satirical `தோலத் தரிப்பது` image is translated literally rather than doctrinally softened.

translation.english_text: Listen: just as you have an Ammaiyappan, the people of the world too have an Ammaiyappan.
Where are they, I wonder?—
They cannot be seen by the eye!—
When we, their children, can be seen by the eye, shouldn't the parents be visible too?

Wrong!... Those divine parents cannot be seen—they are formless—possessed of the power to create and destroy all the cosmic spheres... bearers of a thousand names... praised in many an invocatory verse... this world and the next, pleasure and pain... pillar and speck... there... here... shining everywhere... What, Sukhadev... has your confusion ended?...
notes: The source's accumulating devotional catalogue and paired fragments are preserved rather than reorganized into systematic theology.
`பாயிரம்` is rendered as `invocatory verse` for readability while retaining its literary function.

translation.english_text: It is only now beginning.
Oh, Ammaiyappa—
Sukhadev, don't ask mischievous questions like this; trying to trip up holy men in this way is a great sin......
No, Father, I only asked because I did not know. I take it back.......
Good.

Maykainatha Swami......

Maykainatha Swami......

Maykainatha Swami......
Looks as though Maykainatha Swami has had quite a haul.
They are all offerings sent by devotees......
Offerings!... Yes—there is a name like that too for wages received without working...
notes: The satire equates devotional offerings with unearned wages; the English keeps that barb explicit.

translation.english_text:
Well—well—well! Where did you learn such a great truth? Did one of those Eighteen Siddhars you read say it?... Did Kudambai Siddhar say it?

Mutha, don't start your super-intellectual sermon......
notes: The second paragraph remains inside the same immutable Vetha dialogue record, exactly as the verified dialogue layer models it.

translation.english_text: Why do you get angry when I say something about the swami?

Hey, Mutha! This is the post office. People come here and go from here... Your babbling like this is dangerous for me... I knew something like this would happen; that is why I hesitated so much to rent you that room in my house....
All right—all right—I've shut my mouth...
Not enough!... Tuck your tail in too...
What is this—the Ramayana? Ravana's court?......
All right, why are you standing here? Aren't you going to the palace to groom the horse?......
Why—are you afraid that if I stay here I'll keep talking about something or other?...

No. Shouldn't you work properly at the place that pays you wages? That's why I said it.... You're a good boy—go ruin yourself however you like. My duty matters to me. Only don't say anything about the swami. He isn't a choultry loafer like you; he is a saint renowned throughout the world.
notes: `சத்திரத்துப் பேர்வழி` is rendered as `choultry loafer` to retain the period social insult rather than smoothing it into a generic `vagabond`.

translation.english_text: A saint renowned throughout the world! It seems even such a great saint has not gained the power to win freedom for this Pazhuthar, which remains enslaved...?...

Why should he care about the freedom of Pazhuthar?... Is he a man of narrow vision like you? His broad aim is for people to gain deliverance from this sinful world and go to the other world... 'Freedom for Pazhuthar'—some freedom!......

Let the younger queen Poongavanam marry the ruler of Vengai today; tomorrow Pazhuthar will have its freedom.
notes: The contrast between political `விடுதலை` and religious deliverance is preserved rather than harmonized into one register.

translation.english_text: Is an unwilling marriage the price to be paid for freedom?
All right—all right—I can't talk to you! Ah, great freedom fighter!... See to your work... I'm coming.

source_locator.description: Opening bracketed action after the decorative star.

translation.english_text: [Poongavanam is gathering fruit for Muthan.]
Poongavanam—Poongavanam.......

source_locator.description: Exact source form begins `பூங் ;`; the semicolon is evidence and is not normalized.

translation.english_text: What is it, brother... what is the news?.......
notes: This is the post-closure scene-3 source-role supplement. The Tamil evidence remains the exact semicolon form `பூங் ; ...`; English metadata does not convert it into a colon-labelled source record.

translation.english_text: News! After being born with a brother like me, what other news could I have? Look—the king of Vengai has sent a palm-leaf message......
As always, it is about my marriage, isn't it?......
Marriage? He has forgotten that now... The message that has come now... is for fifty thousand gold coins... an urgent order. The tribute must be paid, Poongavanam... the tribute must be paid...
notes: `அரை லட்சம்` is rendered numerically by sense as fifty thousand, without changing the Tamil source wording.

translation.english_text: This is nothing unusual, is it, brother!...

Usual? Poongavanam, think.... If you had agreed to marry that ruler of Vengaipuram, how many lakhs of gold would have remained with us over these fifteen years? I have poured it out and wept, into the seat of that tyrant's rule......
notes: `லட்சம்` is retained as `lakhs` here because the speaker's accumulation is rhetorical rather than a single amount needing conversion.

translation.english_text: For that... can I change my opinion?......
Opinion—what a grand opinion!.... For years the king of Vengai city tried to marry you and in the end took a vow of celibacy.... And you hate him......
Brother... this is neither the time nor the age for me to talk of marriage... Please let me live in peace... I don't want that wretched marriage talk! I absolutely do not want it.
By crying and crying like this, you've ruined Pazhuthar itself... What use is there in talking to you......

source_locator.description: Opening scene-setting prose after the decorative star.

translation.english_text: [Maykainatha Swami is seated on a gold-polished dais. Nearby are Baladevar, his wife and Sukhadev; the guard Tirisangu; the others stand.]

Didn't I tell you about great saints yesterday? Great saints do not appear often. But when such saints do appear, there is nothing they cannot do... They will dry up the sea; they will float in kasanthi... They will speak with God... They will make sugarcane taste bitter; they will make even a crow sing a Gandharva melody... Such are those endowed with divine grace. Warriors and men of wisdom have fame only on earth... But great saints have fame even in heaven. That is why I say: do not touch sword or spear; worship the fragrance of Vaikuntha. Do not bear a shield in your hand. Bear the sacred ash of the Lord of Kailasa... Who are you? Who am I? Mother, father, elder brother, younger brother—all are vain; in the end, a handful of earth.

english_page_segments.english_text: Didn't I tell you about great saints yesterday? Great saints do not appear often. But when such saints do appear, there is nothing they cannot do... They will dry up the sea; they will float in kasanthi... They will speak with God... They will make sugarcane taste bitter; they will make even a crow sing—

a Gandharva melody... Such are those endowed with divine grace. Warriors and men of wisdom have fame only on earth... But great saints have fame even in heaven. That is why I say: do not touch sword or spear; worship the fragrance of Vaikuntha. Do not bear a shield in your hand. Bear the sacred ash of the Lord of Kailasa... Who are you? Who am I? Mother, father, elder brother, younger brother—all are vain; in the end, a handful of earth.

notes: The verified Tamil `கசந்திலே` is not silently repaired; `kasanthi` is retained in transliteration because the frozen source layer does not authorize collapsing it to a guessed English object.

source_locator.description: Bracketed departure after Maykainatha's sermon.

translation.english_text: [Everyone receives sacred ash and leaves.]

source_locator.description: Bracketed arrival of Boopathi.

translation.english_text: [Boopathi enters.]
Come, Boopathi... come. It has been many years since I saw you! Your beard has gone completely white.
Yes!
A tender leaf becomes a dry leaf, after all. What is surprising about a beard turning white?
You said one thing—and said it well. True; as clear as a gooseberry in the palm...
Well, Boopathiyar, how were your travels abroad? I imagine your medical practice has improved many times over since before—your travels were useful for that, weren't they?—
Certainly they were. Twenty years of ceaseless wandering did not go to waste—the truth that what cannot be cured by magic and mantra can be cured by medicine......
Ammaiyappa—there is nothing God cannot do.

source_locator.description: Bracketed arrival of Vedalam.

translation.english_text: [Vedalam enters.]
Swami, namaste.
What is it, Vedalam?
Many offerings have come for Swamigal. I brought them...
Offerings... Long live the devotees! How much, Vedalam?
Countless gold coins.
Delightful! There is the offering box.

source_locator.description: Bracketed departure of Vedalam.

translation.english_text: [Vedalam leaves.]
Does the Swami never touch gold?
Poison—poison!!......
And isn't this tree growing in that very poison!... Swami! I have returned from abroad; you must give me a gift—will you?
A gift? What, Boopathi?
You must show that treasure to my eyes.
Treasure?
Not gold or diamonds, Swami... I'm asking for the secret buried within you...
Secret!
Yes. Won't you tell me at least now?
Don't take my life; you were away for twenty years—why have you come here now, man...?

I'll tell you why I came. You too have been living for twenty years hiding that secret! Ha—ha—ha—Swami, even if a horse hides its feed in a sack while it eats, does that mean we won't know it is kol, the horse gram? Ha—ha—ha!
notes: The source's `கொள்` feed term is retained as `kol` with an inline gloss; the joke is not replaced by an invented English pun.

source_locator.description: Opening action prose after the decorative star.

translation.english_text: A horse is eating horse gram. A boy slowly approaches, glancing around furtively... Then he puts his hand into the feed sack, takes some horse gram and eats it himself... Tirisangu comes there... A blow lands on the boy's head...

source_locator.description: Exact source form begins `திரு;`; the semicolon is evidence and is not normalized.

translation.english_text: You thieving donkey—who the hell are you! What are you staring at—spit it out... mm... spit!... Will you come here again, eh...
notes: The rough abuse is retained without euphemism. The Tamil evidence remains the exact source form `திரு; ...`, not a normalized colon-labelled record.

source_locator.description: Bracketed action as Muthan arrives during the beating.

translation.english_text: [Muthan comes and catches hold.]
notes: The source does not require an English object for `பிடித்துக் கொள்கிறான்`; none is invented.

translation.english_text: Why... are you hitting him?......
So you've come to plead for him, have you... Mutha—what a fine way you look after the horses! Every little thieving brat is coming right inside the palace to steal!
If this hungry boy, unable to bear his hunger, ate a little horse gram—is that theft? In this world, all sorts of people steal all sorts of things...
Right, then. Looks as though you'll divide up the Palayakkarar's property and hand it to the hungry yourself.
notes: `பாளையக்காரர்` is retained as the period title `Palayakkarar` rather than flattened into a generic modern office.

translation.english_text: Even if I don't, that time is bound to come. Here, little brother—you run along......

source_locator.description: Parenthetical action after Muthan tells the boy to run.

translation.english_text: [He takes some horse gram and gives it to him.]
Kaveri is such a good woman—and a boy like this had to be born from her belly!......

source_locator.description: Parenthetical departure followed by the arrival of a warrior.

translation.english_text: [He leaves. A warrior enters.]
Mutha!... Kumar Raja is coming—to learn swordsmanship.......
Who's that! Kumar Raja? All right!......
Yes! Prince Sukhadev......

Prince, Kumar Raja!... As if he's someone different—he just keeps flinging out new titles...... Hey, at least look at the merit before showering him with titles; what now... is he going to learn swordplay and win freedom for Pazhuthar?...... What a mighty hero of heroes... All right... all right... go... I'm coming.
notes: The exaggerated honorific pile-up and Muthan's sarcasm are preserved rather than normalized into neutral narration.

translation.english_text:
I am a hero among heroes—let enemies come from any side; I will face them and crush them... Let armies come by the akroni count! I will smash them like pots. Let them lay siege to forts... let them enter the audience hall itself... I will resist... drive them off... strike... pound the enemies of the world to dust... reduce all the chariots, elephants, cavalry and infantry to powder. Hmm... yes... which hand holds the shield, and which hand holds the sword... Hey, just tell me that much, will you?

(Muthan enters.

Ah!... He'll know. Mutha!... Within two days I must become a great swordsman.
notes: The frozen source record itself contains the parenthetical Muthan-arrival cue inside Sukhadev's immutable dialogue span; English preserves it inside this one linked unit rather than splitting or duplicating the source record.
The source form `அக்ரோணிக்` is carried as `akroni` rather than silently repaired to a familiar epic military term.

translation.english_text: Oh... we can make you into a swordsman.
What! A swordsman?...
Ah, it slipped out wrong. Never mind... You've heard of the sword-hero Hanuman, haven't you?......

Yes... yes, the one who went to Sita in Ashoka Grove...

All right... all right... come...

source_locator.description: Parenthetical sword-practice action after Sukhadev tells Muthan to come.

translation.english_text: [They begin swordplay; Muthan starts whirling his sword a little faster......]

source_locator.description: Unlabelled line after the first sword-practice cue; resolved to Sukhadev by the closed source-role review.

translation.english_text: Hmm.... Will this work with him?
notes: Speaker identity comes from the closed source-role supplement; no printed speaker label is invented.

source_locator.description: Parenthetical cue that the fight resumes.

translation.english_text: [They fight again.]

source_locator.description: Unlabelled speech after the renewed fight; resolved to Sukhadev by the closed source-role review.

translation.english_text: Hey... wait... wait! It'll strike somewhere it shouldn't and somebody will get killed... Give me that...
notes: Speaker identity is derivative provenance only; the Tamil evidence remains unlabelled at this point.

source_locator.description: Bracketed action fetching a long sword and dagger.

translation.english_text: [He himself goes and brings a long sword and a dagger, looking at the warrior standing there.]
Hey... you go.

source_locator.description: Parenthetical addressee cue before the next source-role-resolved Sukhadev line.

translation.english_text: [To Muthan.]

source_locator.description: Unlabelled line immediately after the `(முத்தனிடம்)` cue; resolved to Sukhadev by the closed source-role review.

translation.english_text: Here... hold this... Now let's see who wins...
notes: The preceding addressee cue is preserved separately; it does not become a printed speaker label.

translation.english_text: Wait. This is no way to conduct a fight......
I don't need any rules.

source_locator.description: Sword strike hits Muthan and Poongavanam runs over.

translation.english_text: [He swings the sword at Muthan. It strikes him. Seeing this, Poongavanam runs over......]
Sukhadev!...... What is this reckless game?
Swordplay. Why are you interfering in this, aunt? Mutha! Put medicine on the wound; I'm going.

source_locator.description: Sukhadev leaves and Poongavanam immediately tears cloth to bandage Muthan.

translation.english_text: [Sukhadev leaves. At once Poongavanam tears a strip of cloth and binds the wound....]
Young Queen...
notes: The exact Tamil speaker label includes the source parenthetical `(திகிலுடன்)`; it remains unchanged in provenance rather than being normalized to `முத்`.

translation.english_text: It's all right, Mutha. I'll bandage it myself.

source_locator.description: Poongavanam's eyes fill with tears.

translation.english_text: [Tears well in her eyes....]
Yuva Rani, you seem somehow different...
notes: The period address `யுவராணி` is retained as `Yuva Rani` instead of being flattened into a generic modern title.

translation.english_text:
It's nothing, Mutha... Here, eat this. I'm going—someone may come...

[She gives him the fruit she had kept hidden and leaves. Muthan stands bewildered with the fruit.]
notes: The frozen immutable dialogue record includes the trailing unlabelled action prose; English keeps it inside this one linked unit rather than duplicating source ownership as a second stage-direction unit.

source_locator.description: Opening action before Sukhadev's first labelled utterance.

translation.english_text: [Sukhadev admires his beauty in the mirror. Tirisangu comes there with a letter.]
This mirror isn't enough to behold my beauty, haa-m—Tirisangu! A palm-leaf letter for me?
notes: The immutable Tamil record itself contains the string `திரிசங்கு:` inside Sukhadev's labelled turn. English treats it as Sukhadev calling to Tirisangu rather than splitting or repairing the locked source record.

translation.english_text: No, thambi. It's for me.
From whom?
He's an idle fellow. Once day breaks, his one job is to take my life.
Take your life? Who is that Yama, man?
Ask me, thambi. I have a good-for-nothing nephew. Says he wants a woman.
Why? Are all those being born nowadays male?
No, thambi, no. He wants a woman for marriage.
For marriage, of course you need a woman. What else do you need? That's the raw material of a wedding, isn't it?
Thambi! The mango fruit itself is calling, ‘Bats, come!’
Yes! Yes! A ripe mango and a ruined hall don't need to call, ‘Bat, come.’ All right, likewise......

My daughter has come of age. Fellows are shooting their bows; that's why I've written a palm-leaf letter to this useless fellow. My daughter's beauty, her character—can this fellow claim a right over her merely because of the aththan kinship, thambi?
notes: `அத்தான் முறை` is retained as `aththan kinship` rather than forcing a modern relationship gloss beyond what the frozen source itself establishes.

translation.english_text: Oh-ho! Is your daughter that beautiful—
Haven't you ever seen her?
No. What's your daughter's name?
Muthayi—Muthayi means Muthayi.
Hmm—even a crow thinks its chick is a golden chick.
No, thambi. This is a koel's chick that a crow has brooded.
Tirisangu! Come, let's go to your house.
Don't joke—the prince coming to a palace guard's house... what a joke, what a joke.
Don't you know I have none of that high-and-low with me? You're a servant only to my younger sister. To me, you're an elderly friend. Right?
I am fortunate.
Come, let's go.

source_locator.description: Source cue that the Muthan–Muthayi love-song performance is nearing its end; no title or lyric body is printed.

translation.english_text: [As the Muthan–Muthayi love-song performance is nearing its end, Sumathi arrives carrying two water pots, one on either side at her waist. She sets the pots at a distance, looks at Muthan and Muthayi, covers both her eyes with her hands, and comes toward them.]
notes: The booklet prints no title or lyric lines for this occurrence. The unresolved item-level authorship state is preserved and no soundtrack lyric is reconstructed.

translation.english_text: Muthayi! Shall we go?
What, Sumathi! Why have you closed your eyes?

source_locator.description: Bracketed cue that Sumathi opens her eyes.

translation.english_text: [Opening her eyes.]
For a reason. It's getting late. Come, let's go.
Shall I go and come back?
You won't get just that permission over there.
Well, your friend seems to be quite a clever-handed woman.
Not just a ‘handy one’—a foot one, a neck one, a head one too.
notes: The source deliberately piles up `கைக்காரி / கால்காரி / கழுத்துக்காரி / தலைக்காரி`; the English keeps the comic body-part sequence rather than normalizing it away.

translation.english_text: Enough! Enough! Don't keep spitting ‘kaari, kaari’ in my face.
notes: The phonetic joke on repeated `காரி` is retained in transliteration rather than replaced with a different English pun.

translation.english_text: All right! I'm coming. Hey, Sumathi! Turn that way for a moment. I'll be right there.

source_locator.description: Final source cue while Sumathi stands turned away.

translation.english_text: [As Sumathi stands turned away, a sound—‘ich’—echoes on Sumathi's face.]
notes: The source's theatrical image is preserved without adding an explicit kissing action that the printed cue itself does not state.

source_locator.description: Opening source cue before the first labelled dialogue.

translation.english_text: [Muthayi comes carrying a water pot.]
Muthayi!... Muthayi!
What is it, appa?......
Where did you go, girl? How many places am I supposed to search for you... See who's come... Thambi, come in. Shoo... shoo... who called you in...?
notes: The abrupt `சீ...சீ...` is carried as a shooing interjection rather than normalized into explanatory prose.

source_locator.description: Source cue: a goat enters, followed by Sukhadev.

translation.english_text: [A goat comes in; Sukhadev follows it.]

source_locator.description: Unlabelled invitation after the goat/Sukhadev arrival cue; resolved to Tirisangu by the closed source-role review.

translation.english_text: Come in, thambi!... Don't be shy, girl... there's no one else... This is Prince Sukhadev.
notes: Speaker identity comes from the closed source-role supplement; no printed label is invented in the Tamil evidence layer.

translation.english_text: Greetings!...

Long life!... Long life!... Ah!... The way those hands fold and unfold looks like a lotus flower. Tirisangu, everything you said is true... Oh, poor thing! Her cheeks have reddened with shyness, like ripe chillies—

source_locator.description: Muthayi goes inside after Sukhadev's teasing.

translation.english_text: [Muthayi goes inside.]
Should you tease her like this the moment you see her, thambi?
Eh... what did I say?... Did I say something without realizing it?... Hmm... Tirisangu, I want to ask you one thing... you won't refuse, will you...
You are Palayakkarar Baladevar's son... the prince... I am merely your servant. You have the right to take without even asking....
Aha-ha... tch... tch... my eyes are spinning... my ears refuse to hear... my tongue says it won't move... ayyayyo! My heart isn't beating at all......
Thambi!... Thambi!... What is this... Shall I go bring the physician....?
No, no. This is an illness with no medicine... ‘when eye looks with eye...’... that is, I have fallen like a fly into the toddy-pot called love!

english_page_segments.english_text: No, no. This is an illness with no medicine... ‘when eye looks with eye...’... that—
—is, I have fallen like a fly into the toddy-pot called love!

notes: The source itself prints only the fragmentary `கண்ணொடு கண்ணோக் கொக்கின் ...`; English preserves that incompleteness and does not repair the quotation from an external text.

translation.english_text: Thambi!... Go today and come tomorrow; the matter will succeed......

‘Go today, come tomorrow’... Ah! I feel I've heard those words somewhere... Hmm... yes, in the Kamba Ramayanam... Rama says exactly that to Ravana... Ayyo! Ravana came back the next day and did not get victory; didn't he get death instead......
But the Rama who came the next day won, didn't he, thambi...
Oh!... Then this Rama will definitely come tomorrow...
Do come for certain...
Would I stay away?—Tirisangu's house is a lotus pond; the bee that flies there is this Sukhadev... I'm going now, Tirisangu...
All right, thambi!...

source_locator.description: Sukhadev leaves; Tirisangu turns angry.

translation.english_text: [He leaves. Tirisangu, angrily:]
Muthayi!... Muthayi!...
What, appa! Has that man gone?...
Man?...
No... no... forgive me; I misspoke...
Forgive you?... The prince himself came to the house... Is this how you insult him?...
The prince... hmm... a bad young man...
Who is bad? Is he lacking in beauty?... Lacking in status?... Foolish girl—you cannot grasp his intelligence...
Perhaps this noble man's intelligence is smaller than the point of a needle—too small to grasp! Isn't that so, appa?...
Enough, stop. If he wished, even Urvashi and Rambha would come running...
What's surprising about that, appa? Those who came running even to the sages of the royal court—would they say no if palace men called them? They'll come, appa, they'll come—
Shut your mouth, you chatterbox! I begged and coaxed him and brought him home; you sent him away with soot smeared on his face.
No—he left too soon! Appa! Appa! If you smeared soot on his face he'd look even more handsome, like the dark-cloud-hued one.
Careful—if that reaches his ears, he'll pluck out your eyes.
notes: The exact Tamil speaker label is `திருசங்கு` here; it is retained as source provenance rather than normalized to another spelling.

translation.english_text: Is he Kannappa Nayanar?
Tch! An answer for every word.

source_locator.description: Final source action: Muthayi laughs and runs inside.

translation.english_text: [Muthayi laughs and runs inside.]
When there are thousands of soldiers, and when a brave commander like you, Velazhagar, is here, whom is the king of Vengai city afraid of that he is increasing the army still further?

The army is being enlarged not out of fear... but for protection, Baladevar. Siruthaiyuran is waiting for when he can pounce on Vengai city, for whatever pretext will give him a battlefield. That is why our king has ordered us to set about enlarging the army and build a barrier.
notes: The frozen source phrase `தடைகட்டாடென` is rendered by its immediate sentence sense; the Tamil source itself is not corrected or normalized.

translation.english_text: I am waiting to do whatever I can.
You will. But your townspeople may dislike joining the forces on the Vengai side. After all, is he not the king who has made them slaves?
That's nothing. I, the first slave, prostrate full-length before him. With all my heart I pray to God that he may live. As you expect, many will join the army. There is no doubt.
All right! I must go to your place.
The Thendral Palace on South Raja Street has been arranged for you.
Excellent.
Thambi! Thambi! Ever since you came to my house... goodness! From that moment Muthayi has talked of nothing but you.
What—what—wait, wait—is that so? Here, Tirisangu! Here—here! There are a hundred gold coins in this... keep it... hmm... what does she say—what does she say—
Muthayi says, thambi, that there is bravery in your walk—a majesty in your gaze—sweetness in your speech—and she said there's something in your hand.
notes: The exact source speaker-label spelling `திருசங்கு` is retained in provenance.

translation.english_text: A finger—a finger!
No, thambi...
There's a ring on the finger...
Not that, thambi—oh, go on—what do I know about all this wretched love-description business?
notes: The frozen source form `இந்த எழவு காதல் வாணமெல்லாமா தெரியுது` is translated by immediate contextual sense without changing the Tamil wording.

translation.english_text: Then Muthayi is in love with me. Ah, Tirisangu! If there were a father like you, and that father had a daughter like Muthayi, the world would very soon become a grove of love without opposition. Muthayi! You and I... Ayyo, I don't even know how to describe it, Tirisangu! Is there a Kamba Ramayanam in our library?
What, thambi! What connection is there between love and the Kamba Ramayanam?

source_locator.description: Immutable Sukhadev dialogue containing the source-attributed Kambar verse fragment; linked to song/performance inventory occurrence without duplicating source ownership.

translation.english_text:
Ayyayyo! Three-quarters of the Ramayanam is just that. Ah! Do you know how the emperor of poets, Kambar, described love?... Listen to a song, Tirisangu...

‘After “the cloud-dark one who came with the great sage”... by the fact that he was lotus-eyed... yes... her doubt fell away: “Could it be he?”... vāmamēkalaiyi vaḷarntatu...’

Hmm, gone—I forgot beyond that... Come, come, let's look it up.
notes: The immediate source dialogue explicitly attributes the quotation to Kambar. Only the fragment printed in this booklet is translated; no canonical Kambar verse is reconstructed from outside material.
The final frozen source cluster `வாமமேகலையி வளர்ந்தது` is retained in transliteration because this printed quotation is fragmentary and the source itself immediately says the rest has been forgotten.
This one unit owns both the immutable dialogue record and `ammaiyappan-song-002` occurrence linkage, preventing duplicate source-span ownership.

translation.english_text: You are gold that cannot be found even by searching... Father is trying to separate me from you.

Your father is right to think that way, isn't he? Where is Prince Sukhadev—and where am I? I am a man who rubs down horses in the palace... motherless... not knowing who my father is... without kin or relatives... a man alone.
Man alone... The stars may gather in crowds. The moon stands alone. But isn't it the moon that the water-lily waits for?
My lily—your father dreams of becoming kin to the Palayakkarar. Is he going to give you to this paari? A dream... a dream...
notes: The frozen source word `பாரிக்கா` is not silently repaired; `paari` is retained because its exact intended sense is not independently resolved by the source layer.

translation.english_text: I will make even the dream come true. My dear... leave your worries... look at me; won't you look? Isn't my face medicine that can cure your worry?

source_locator.description: Muthan looks at her; both smile.

translation.english_text: [Muthan looks at her. Both smile.]

Medicine indeed... my Manikkavalli! Medicine that cures worry... this guileless silver moon. How many cruel nights, drunk on the taste of sorrow, have slipped away without a word, Sundari... simply because I thought of your radiant face... I would pine, thinking, 'Am I not poor?' Then my eyes, still unable to know the limits of your beauty, would ask: 'Are you poor—you who possess a jewel no pauper or mansion-dweller could ever obtain?' My joy! You are medicine that cures my pain... a feast without equal....

source_locator.description: The lovers embrace.

translation.english_text: [They embrace.]
Shh... don't go flying.
Would a skylark not fly at the touch of spring?
One wing is not enough to fly.
That is why I am inviting you too.
Yes! Where shall we fly?
To the edge of the blue sky, between the beautifully arrayed clouds—above the waterfall—around the lovely grove—

source_locator.description: Muthayi laughs.

translation.english_text: [She laughs.]

source_locator.description: Unlabelled question after Muthayi's laugh continues Muthan's turn.

translation.english_text: Why are you laughing, Muthayi?

I have heard it said... that poet... lover... madman... all three are one kind. A poet looks at the sky and the lotus and picks a quarrel: 'Hey, stars! At whom are you winking?' A lover looks at the white moon, laments, 'Where is my beloved?' and asks the moon to carry a message. People joke that both of them are mad... Looking at you, it really does seem true...

source_locator.description: Muthayi touches Muthan.

translation.english_text: [She touches him.]
Hush... don't touch me... I'm the madman, after all.
Even if you are mad, aren't you my Muthan? Piththa! Pirai-kudi! Perumane!
notes: The devotional-sounding source phrase `பித்தா! பிறைகுடி! பெருமானே!` is translated partly by transliteration and is not repaired to a more familiar hymn wording.

source_locator.description: Muthayi touches him again.

translation.english_text: [She touches him.]
Shh... amma. Wait, Muthayi.
Why! If I touch you, will it turn into sacred ash?

source_locator.description: Muthayi touches him once more.

translation.english_text: [She touches him.]
Shh... amma. Wait, Muthayi.
That's it!

source_locator.description: Sukhadev and Tirisangu appear.

translation.english_text: [Sukhadev and Tirisangu.]
Ah! Right... right... maal nannoram... at the edge of the grove...
notes: The frozen phrase `மால் நன்னோரம்` is left in transliteration rather than silently reconstructed.

translation.english_text: Prince! Please don't misunderstand. This fellow has started forcing himself on my girl. Hey, brainless wretch! What are you doing?
Father!
Don't be afraid, girl—he won't do anything to me. He's just a lazy fellow who frightens women.
No, father.

source_locator.description: Source action word `திருக்கிட்டு` after Muthayi's denial.

translation.english_text: [Tirukkittu.]
notes: The frozen action word `திருக்கிட்டு` is retained in transliteration because the source layer does not establish a single safe English action.

translation.english_text: I understand everything myself... Why do you come to places like this alone?
Listen to what I have to say.
You needn't say anything; go home, girl... Don't stand in front of this sinner... it's wrong... go, girl—are you going or not? Hm... go...

source_locator.description: Muthayi leaves distressed.

translation.english_text: [Muthayi leaves, distressed.]

source_locator.description: Prayer/address after Muthayi leaves continues Tirisangu's preceding turn.

translation.english_text: God! You have saved my daughter's honour... a crore salutations to you... Prince! Did you see this fellow's outrage?

source_locator.description: Source cue: Muthan is struck/tapped on the back.

translation.english_text: [Muthan is struck on the back.]
Hey, Mutha! Is your back muttering? You half-starved mendicant brat! You whining donkey.
Had enough, agathi?
notes: The insult/term `அகாதி` is retained as `agathi`; the frozen source does not authorize a confident normalization.

translation.english_text: Don't talk... you cowardly dog! You have no way even to get half a belly of gruel, and yet you go about loving—love indeed.

Rich man's son! You who do not know the difference between the heart and the stomach! I'll teach you the grammar of love... listen... Love is not saying, 'I will bathe in rosewater, swim in fruit juice, and go to and fro from a bedchamber surrounded by maidens'... Love is a moon... a breeze... It comes not only to the mansion but to the mud hut too... Love is not money; it does not stop at your marble hall...
That's right, fellow; you cannot hide your villainy behind too much clever talk.
How could I? For that, one would have to be born the son of a Palayakkarar...
Shut up! You father-name-unknown mistake.
notes: The source's unusual insult `தகப்பன் பெயர் தெரியாத தவறுதலில்` is kept deliberately awkward rather than normalized into a smoother invented epithet.

translation.english_text: Do you know your father's name?

source_locator.description: Muthan and Sukhadev fight.

translation.english_text: [The two of them fight.]

source_locator.description: Narrated fight outcome and Sukhadev's fall into the water.

translation.english_text: Sukhadev's cap flies upward and falls. A blow from Muthan knocks Sukhadev down. He gets up, bravely takes the walking stick Tirisangu is holding, advances as though to strike Muthan, retrieves his cap caught on a tree, warns Muthan, 'Hey, Mutha—careful; be careful!', and falls into the water.
notes: The warning remains embedded in the source narration because it is not a separate immutable labelled-dialogue record.

translation.english_text: Come... come... you're Vedalam, aren't you?
Yes.
Why have you got a name like Vedalam? Did your father and mother read the story of Vikramaditya?
They did; they did—why?

There is a vedalam in the story of Vikramaditya—you must have been born while they were reading it, so they named you Vedalam. Good thing you weren't born while they were reading the Kishkindha Kandam. Come! Come!
notes: `வேதாளம்` is both the character's name and the legendary being in the Vikramaditya story; the wordplay is preserved.

source_locator.description: Velazhagan enters; Vedalam and the warrior bow.

translation.english_text: [Velazhagan enters; Vedalam and the warrior bow.]
My lord! This is Vedalam, whom you sent for.
Oh! Vedalam! Come. I have heard a great deal about you. Baladevar too said you were very capable. You know why I have come—to recruit men for the army. For that, you too...
Me? Ayyo! I don't even have the strength to lift a sword.
You needn't join the army, man... Just catch and bring us some men. There must be plenty of people without work.
But people will be afraid to join the army.
Even a goat is afraid to come to the sacrificial altar. That is why they sprinkle turmeric-water, scatter flowers, hold food out in front and tempt it; one has to make an effort.
Exactly right; I'll begin the work as you order. One more request.
What?
There is a great holy man in this town. Everyone regards his words as divine speech. If we ask him to campaign for men to join the army, our work will become easy.
Do we have to give him anything to receive his grace?
Anything? He will never accept it. He does not even touch material wealth with his hand. There is a donation box at the monastery. It has to be put in there.

source_locator.description: Baladevar's wife and Poongavanam play sokkattan; Sukhadev comes down from upstairs; Tirisangu is at work.

translation.english_text: [Baladevar's wife and Poongavanam are playing sokkattan. Sukhadev comes down from upstairs. Tirisangu is occupied with some work.]
notes: The game name `சொக்கட்டான்` is retained as `sokkattan`.

translation.english_text: Tirisangu! Success! Victory... victory upon victory!
What is it, thambi?
Father has agreed. He has given the order to dismiss Muthan from his job.
What! Dismiss Muthan? Why? What for?
Tch... what for? He grabbed and pulled the hand of our Tirisangu's daughter, Muthayi. I rebuked him. A proper slap on the cheek.
What?
Ah! Ah! I gave it to him.
Are you boasting about that? Does beating a poor man give you some thrill?

source_locator.description: Sukhadev rubs his back.

translation.english_text: [He rubs his back.]
Hm—you don't know what happened, aunt. If you knew, you wouldn't talk like this.
Sukhadev! Don't dismiss Muthan. Who does he have apart from us? Poor orphan—where will he go?
Aunt! You, who chose not to marry and remain a maiden—why don't you think of God and roll your japa beads? Why get into all this trouble?
Sister-in-law, did you hear the way your son speaks?
Sukhadev! Be quiet.
All right, all right! Come, Tirisangu.

source_locator.description: Poongavanam's face falls.

translation.english_text: [Poongavanam looks crestfallen.]

source_locator.description: Muthan checks a sword; Poongavanam arrives.

translation.english_text: Muthan is checking a sword. Poongavanam comes there....
Mutha!...
Young queen! What do you want?...
Nothing... about you and Sukhadev...
Yes, Rani... in a fit of anger, something happened....
Hm... who is that Muthayi?...
[Startled; silent...]
notes: The immutable dialogue record itself consists of a parenthetical reaction; it remains dialogue-kind because source ownership is locked to `ammaiyappan-s014-d006`.

translation.english_text: Won't you tell me?... Who is she who has stolen your heart?... Is she beautiful?... a woman of rare virtue?... a beauty suited to you?... Won't you tell me?... Mutha!... For that girl—have you and the prince fought a great war?...
My lady!....
Do you know what your quarrel has led to?... Your very job is in danger... This sinner is going to lose even the blessing of being able to look at you...
Young queen!...
Don't call me that...

source_locator.description: Sukhadev's voice is heard; Poongavanam hides; Tirisangu arrives.

translation.english_text: [Sukhadev's voice is heard. Poongavanam hides. Tirisangu enters.]
What—oppose me?... Are there human beings in all the fourteen—sixteen worlds who can oppose me? What, Tirisangu...
notes: The source's comic `ஈரேழு பதினறு லோகத்திலும்` is preserved as the odd 'fourteen—sixteen worlds' formulation rather than normalized.

translation.english_text: Uh-uh...
Why stop at eleven worlds? There are no humans in the lunar sphere... none in the solar sphere... none in the realm of the stars...
None, thambi... none... there isn't a single person who can oppose you...

There is one—he too is finished; ...who?... this Muthan... Hey, Mutha!... For the crime you committed there will be no case... inquiry... judgment... none of it... accept the punishment...... You have no job here anymore...
Thank you...

Thank you?... I cannot accept it. Take it back... Tirisangu... not just palace work—announce it throughout the town!... No one anywhere under our authority is to give this fellow work... If they do—I'll cut off the tail... skin the hide... break the leg... tear up the palm-leaf...
Why!... Is there no more 'O' left to say?... You could say, 'I'll tear apart the garland'!
notes: The source runs a comic chain of threats and wordplay; the English keeps the literal escalation without inventing a replacement pun.

translation.english_text: What... what... tear apart the garland?... Am I a monkey? Hm... hey, Mutha! Another great war between you and me is about to begin... Leave the palace immediately and respectfully!... You donkey who doesn't know your father's name!...

source_locator.description: Seeing Muthan's anger, Sukhadev quickly leaves.

translation.english_text: [Seeing Muthan's anger, Sukhadev quickly leaves.]
Come!... Tirisangu!...

source_locator.description: Muthan stands stunned; Poongavanam comes forward.

translation.english_text: [Muthan stands stunned. Poongavanam comes forward.]
Mutha!... Before you go, come by my mansion and then leave!... Don't forget... you must come... you absolutely must come...

source_locator.description: Poongavanam leaves; Muthan remains confused as her words echo repeatedly.

translation.english_text: [She leaves. Muthan is thoroughly confused... Poongavanam's words echo again and again in his mind...]
My whole life has become a confusion...

What lives here! Confusion here too! Love-stricken... a cow seeking its calf... a tiger in deerskin! How splendid the thought—how beautiful the art... Are those works of thought merely consolation to her?... Poongavanam has seen those living paintings... Yet now she keeps looking at them. Her eyes repeatedly circle back toward the doorway, listening for the sound of footsteps. Her heart beats with the longing: will Muthan come?... Ah!... there he is. (Muthan has come.)

english_page_segments.english_text: What lives here! Confusion here too! Love-stricken... a cow seeking its calf... a tiger in deerskin! How splendid the thought—how beautiful the art... Are those works of thought merely consolation to her?...

Poongavanam has seen those living paintings... Yet now she keeps looking at them. Her eyes repeatedly circle back toward the doorway, listening for the sound of footsteps. Her heart beats with the longing: will Muthan come?... Ah!... there he is. (Muthan has come.)

notes: The fragmentary opening `காதல்புறு ... கன்றைநாடும் பசு ... மான்தோல் வேங்கை!` is translated fragmentarily and is not reconstructed into a smoother external or remembered text.

source_locator.description: Muthan enters hesitantly.

translation.english_text: [Muthan enters hesitantly.]
Come... Mutha, come...
Why did you call me?...
I'll tell you—come!...
No, I'll stay right here...

source_locator.description: Poongavanam runs to Muthan.

translation.english_text: [She runs to him.]
My dear; come near me!...
Mutha... Mutha...
Young queen! This does not become your station... You, who vowed to live as an unmarried maiden, refusing marriage—are you calling me, 'My dear, come'?...
Mutha!... my dear!...

Enough, Yuva Rani! Don't you remember?... When my mother left me alone and devoted herself to palace work—you used to comb and adorn me as a little boy, gather me into your arms and delight in me—are you, of all people, now daring to commit this wrong?...
My joy!... listen to this...
I don't want to hear it... You are the ruler's sister... and I am a horseman... Amma, I have heard the story of Raja Bhartrhari... this is even stranger than that...
Mutha?...

All right, all right... If I stay here any longer, I may be swept into some dangerous corner by this flood of desire that has lain restrained and now surges like this... Hm... If you showed this uncontrollable affection to the king of Vengai Nadu—who, unable to attain you, suffers and has taken a vow of brahmacharya—perhaps this country would at least gain freedom... I am going...
Mutha... stop...
No... a storm has entered Poongavanam; I cannot stand against it, amma, I cannot. I'm leaving!
notes: The source wordplay can invoke both the character name Poongavanam and its literal flower-garden sense; the English retains the name rather than choosing one sense and erasing the other.

translation.english_text: Hm... Muthan... from now on he is only a lifeless husk—; not merely in the palace—he will get no work anywhere under the Palayakkarar's authority.
notes: The unusual source punctuation `—;` is not silently normalized.

translation.english_text: Father! What if he stays in our house until he finds work?

Exactly! I tell you not to play with your food; you say you'll bring that very thing and put it around my neck as a garland. Muthayi! Listen to me. No one would dare walk through a cactus wilderness with his eyes open.
It isn't a cactus wilderness, Father—it's a grove of love.

Shut your mouth—or I'll close my own ears. Love, love, before Tirittira Narayanan; please, girl, have a little mercy. Ours is a family in debt. And that is not all. I am indebted in duty to the prince too—whenever I needed it he gave me money, and I stretched out my hand and took it—even the other day he gave a little gold for the preliminary wedding expenses.

english_page_segments.english_text: Shut your mouth—or I'll close my own ears. Love, love, before Tirittira Narayanan;

please, girl, have a little mercy. Ours is a family in debt. And that is not all. I am indebted in duty to the prince too—whenever I needed it he gave me money, and I stretched out my hand and took it—even the other day he gave a little gold for the preliminary wedding expenses.

notes: The frozen form `திரித்திர நாராயணனிடம்` is retained as `Tirittira Narayanan` rather than silently repaired.

source_locator.description: Tirisangu points to the box.

translation.english_text: [Pointing to the box.]
Father! Must my life be ruined for the sake of wealth? Don't I have the right to choose a man suited to my life, Father?
I have chosen a man suited to your life—with mansions and lofty towers. An iron strongbox itself is coming in search of us—and you run after a beggar's bowl.
Father! I was raised in freedom. Don't turn me into a gambler grasping for the Palayakkarar's property, or into collateral used to pay off your debt, Father.

Enough, Muthayi, enough—I will never consent, while I am alive, to your garlanding that annakkavadi. If you refuse me, your wedding procession can set out only after my funeral procession has gone. Yes! Remember that.
notes: `அன்னக் காவடி` is retained as `annakkavadi`; the source's insult is not replaced with a smoother modern equivalent.

source_locator.description: Muthan and his friends are present.

translation.english_text: [Muthan and his friends are there.]
Remember this—today it is me; tomorrow it may be you; this is how we can be struck in the stomach.
notes: The bodily image in `வயிற்றில் அடிக்கப்படலாம்` is preserved rather than reduced to an abstract economic paraphrase.

translation.english_text: What other way is there for this?...

As long as we are all slaves, there will always be a new authority each day and a petty rule for each man... After making room for the honey, can we still hope for drops of honey?... The man from Vengai Nadu threatens the Pazhuthar Palayakkarar... the Palayakkarar threatens us and vents that anger... the Palayakkarar's son crushes the roses of the house and throws them away, then conducts a king's durbar... Is it wrong for me to question that?... I am a horseman! They are lofty minds atop towers! Hm... slaves a little higher up; that is all!

english_page_segments.english_text: As long as we are all slaves, there will always be a new authority each day and a petty rule for each man...

After making room for the honey, can we still hope for drops of honey?... The man from Vengai Nadu threatens the Pazhuthar Palayakkarar... the Palayakkarar threatens us and vents that anger... the Palayakkarar's son crushes the roses of the house and throws them away, then conducts a king's durbar... Is it wrong for me to question that?... I am a horseman! They are lofty minds atop towers! Hm... slaves a little higher up; that is all!

notes: The source's political metaphors and class contrast are preserved without modernization.

source_locator.description: The friends laugh.

translation.english_text: [The friends laugh...]

source_locator.description: Unlabelled speech after the friends laugh continues Muthan's political address.

translation.english_text: Laughter is no use, friends—we must think. We must turn our Pazhuthar, which has become a spider's web, into a splendid flower garden!...

source_locator.description: Vedalam arrives.

translation.english_text: [Vedalam comes in.]

Change it, man; change it!... You can't even pay the rent for this palm-sized place... and you'll turn Pazhuthar into a flower garden!... turn it into a pushpa forest too—Hey!... who are all you fellows, hm?... what work have you got here?... Hm... uff... go... go...
notes: The comic repetition `பூக்காடு / புஷ்பக் காடு` is kept rather than collapsed.

source_locator.description: The friends leave.

translation.english_text: [They leave.]

source_locator.description: After sending the others away, Vedalam immediately asks Muthan for the rent.

translation.english_text: Hey... Mutha! First give me my rent....
Rent? You're asking at a time like this?...
When else am I to ask?.... When you have money, you give it yourself; when you don't, I have to ask and get it...
I haven't found a single job...
Yes!.... You won't get one hereafter either... so...
Wait a little.
Hey, Mutha! Brainless young man! Is there no way to seek wealth in this world?...
By stealing?...
Tch! You're a sturdy fellow... there's good strength in your body...
I could knock Baladevar down with one blow; is that it?...
Madman!... That's not what I mean—I mean join the army of the people of Vengaipuram!
What? The army?!...
Yes! The Palayakkarar's authority cannot stop it... the renowned spear... Vel the warrior...
notes: The clipped source wordplay around `வேல்` is preserved without expanding an uncertain intended reference.

translation.english_text: Enough... enough... Me, in the army of the overlord who has enslaved us? Tch! Better to die!
Everyone in town is a fool and you're the only wise man?... Maykkainatha Swamiyar himself is going to campaign for the war...
The Swamiyar! Of course he will. He isn't the one who will die in the fighting... that's why!
Enough... don't join the army either. I don't want anything. What is it to me? Just somehow pay my rent. Don't make a good man keep asking—I'm going... to hear the sermon.

source_locator.description: Vedalam leaves.

translation.english_text: [He leaves.]

source_locator.description: Townspeople are gathered; Thanapathi, Velazhagar, doctor Boopathi, Vedalam and others are present; Maykkai Natha Swamigal's speech is in progress.

translation.english_text: [The townspeople are gathered. Thanapathi, Velazhagar, Doctor Boopathi, Vedalam and many others are present. Maykkai Natha Swamigal's speech is in progress.]

Friends! Until now Thanapathi Velazhagar has delivered an instructive speech about the benefits of the army. I too am going to say the same thing. Bhagavan Paranthaman himself told Parthan to take part in the Bharata war. Those who preach today that war must not be fought, that it is a path of frenzy—let them read the Bhagavad Gita. Then they will see how much that flute-player has said about the necessity of war. What do the trident in Siva's hand, the spear of Siva's son, and Vishnu's discus signify? Peace? Or battle? Therefore, friends! All of you become warriors... do not fear death. It is not only by taking up a sword that people die; many have ended their lives by slipping on a banana peel. For a warrior, there is fame not only on earth but in heaven too. Bear the garland of victory upon those bent shoulders. For that, bear swords in your hands. Strike your strong shoulders and set out saying that God is your support... Ammaiyappa! Long live the path of virtue!...
notes: Religious and martial rhetoric is preserved as source rhetoric; no external theological correction is introduced.

translation.english_text: Ammaiyappa! Ammaiyappa!

source_locator.description: The crowd disperses; Thanapathi and the Swamiyar meet in private.

translation.english_text: [The crowd disperses. Thanapathi and the Swamiyar meet in a private place.]
I offer you my deepest thanks.
I did my duty.
If heads of monasteries like you set out to serve the country, both worlds will be illuminated. I will meet you later. I take my leave.
Ammaiyappa! Long live the path of grace.

source_locator.description: Maykkai Nadhar returns near his seat; Doctor Boopathi alone remains seated; seeing him, Maykkai Nadhar is startled.

translation.english_text: [Maykkai Nadhar comes back near his seat. Doctor Boopathi alone is still sitting there. Seeing him, Maykkai Nadhar is startled.]

english_page_segments.english_text: [Maykkai Nadhar comes back near his seat. Doctor Boopathi alone is still sitting there.
Seeing him, Maykkai Nadhar is startled.]

translation.english_text: What, Boopathi! You still haven't left?

I forgot myself, Swamiyare! I lost my very heart in your speech. Hee... hee... hee... 'Do not touch sword or spear—worship the Lord of Vaikuntha... do not bear a shield in your hand—bear the sacred ash of the Lord of Kailasa...' Where is all that now? 'Bear the garland of victory on bent shoulders... for that, bear spears in your hands...' And where is this? Everything is maya... magic illusion... isn't it, Swamiyare?
notes: Boopathi's mocking quotation and contrast are preserved as such.

translation.english_text: Boopathi! Enough, please go.

I am praising you, Swamiyare, praising you! Ahaha! Lord! What all they use you for. Every great man who appears in the world, they say, is your incarnation. They say you incarnated as the Paramatma and told Arjuna to wage war. Then, they say, you yourself incarnated as Bhagavan Buddha and showed Ashoka the good path, saying war is evil. When they have made even you contradict yourself like this, what does this Swamiyar amount to?
Boopathi! If a sadhu is enraged, even the forest cannot contain it, Boopathi!
It is not the sadhu that is trembling... it is deceit, argument, and evil that are trembling.
notes: The rhyming source sequence `சூது, வாது, தீது` is translated semantically; its sound-play is only partly recoverable in English.

translation.english_text: Why should there be any quarrel between us, man....
What is there between us? Tell me that secret.
Boopathi: I bow to you. Please go away. Just don't ask about that secret!
notes: The immutable source record is labelled `மாய்க்கை நாதர்` but its text itself begins `பூபதி:`. That repeated source token is retained in translation rather than silently deleted or reassigned.

translation.english_text: Swamiyare! I'm going. Swamiyare! Remember just one thing. A lie slowly, little by little, grows and blossoms... but truth suddenly explodes... Ha... ha... ha... I'm going.

source_locator.description: Boopathi leaves; the Swamiyar sighs deeply and goes to sit on the seat.

translation.english_text: [Boopathi leaves. The Swamiyar lets out a deep sigh and goes to sit on the seat.]

source_locator.description: The source says Muthan is singing while the post-runner carries bags out and Tirisangu arrives; no title or lyric body is printed.

translation.english_text: [While Muthan is singing, the post-runner carries some bags out. Tirisangu enters.]
notes: The booklet prints only the performance cue. No song title, lyric body, or authorship is reconstructed.

translation.english_text: Where is Muthan? Mutha!
Ah!
Don't be afraid, Mutha.
Why fear! The palace must have issued some new order.
The palace has nothing to do with my coming... Mutha, there is no one here, is there?
No... what is it?
I know that there is true love between you and my daughter.
At least you know it now!
Listen, Mutha! Muthayi has said she cannot marry anyone but you. She has fallen to the bow you shot.
I did not shoot, and she did not fall... We are both doves caught in the net of love!
That net must be cut and my daughter freed. Even after she is freed, you must not remain a vulture chasing her.

She will not be at a distance that needs chasing. Muthayi is a parrot perched on my shoulder! Are you thinking, 'What is this—this son-in-law speaks to his father-in-law without any shyness?' Forgive me.
Listen, Mutha; you are the one who must save my honour. Do you know how I wish my daughter to live?
Our life will go exactly as you wish!

It will not, Mutha. It will not. Do not ruin a family for nothing. You have no means to live; you cannot live. Leave me aside... Would any father, however mad, agree to give his daughter to a poor man like you? Can you run a family? You are a man too; have you lost all shame, to marry and then lie waiting upon your father-in-law's house? Muthayi is a young girl. She does not know the world...... She talks of love now. After marriage, all those love-songs will become stories of the past. Diamond earrings for the ears, a pearl necklace for the neck—that is how women's minds change. Can you buy those for my daughter? Leave running a family aside—do you even have one gold coin to fix the marriage and give the priest dakshina? Mutha! Don't think I am speaking in anger; I will tell you one more thing. You worked at the post-house. That too is gone... You groomed horses for the post-house and, as wages for that, lived in this palm-sized room. You cannot do even that work anymore; the palace order forbids it. From now on the shade of houses and the shade of cattle—those are your dwellings! Mutha! Do not grieve that I am examining your poverty; along with all this grief I will tell you one more thing, so that you may understand. Suppose you were older, used to living in step with the world, and suppose you too had a daughter. Would you give that daughter in marriage to a bridegroom whose father's name was unknown? Perhaps you might. Could I? Would my orthodox mind allow it? Think! You know only that your mother was Kaveri; whom she bore you to is......
