translation.english_text: Muthayi! Muthan will not die...
Is that philosophy spoken in a swami's style?... Are you saying my Muthan will live happily in heaven?... Are you saying only the flower-body perishes, while the body of fame never perishes!...
notes: The source's rhetorical `பூவுடல் / புகழுடல்` pairing is kept visibly parallel rather than normalized into ordinary prose.

translation.english_text: No! Baladevar has gone to meet the emperor—Muthan is certain to be released!...
There!... Father has come too. What happened, father? Is Muthan to be released?...

source_locator.description: Baladevar lowers his head.

translation.english_text: [Baladevar lowers his head.]
Yes, freedom for my Muthan! Freedom from this world for my beloved Muthan! Freedom from this earth where traitors like you live for my dear Muthan! Freedom! Freedom!
notes: The repeated `விடுதலை` is preserved as `freedom`, keeping the bitter double sense of release and death in the source rhetoric.

source_locator.description: Muthayi runs away as though seized by frenzy.

translation.english_text: [She runs off... like one seized by frenzy.]

source_locator.description: The prison door opens and Muthayi runs in.

translation.english_text: [The door opens! Muthayi runs in.]
Aththan!...
notes: `அத்தான்` is retained as `Aththan` because the intimate kinship/lover address is part of the scene's register.

translation.english_text: My joy! Do not be shaken! Today is our last day! Our last meeting!... I can no longer see your eyes that sing of love! I can no longer taste the sweetness of your honey-pouring lips! Only another second or two; after that this poor Muthan can no longer carry within him the sweet memories of you!...
Aththan! No one can ever separate us—I too will come right behind you......

Hmm... madness! Some wishful fool scribbled that a world has been built for lovers and that dead lovers can settle in that world! Do not believe that and follow me! I, who am about to give up my life, ask of you only one loving command...
Whatever it is, ask me...
That you must live, without dying...
Ah!... I am one who cannot live, Aththan—I must not live any longer...

Hmm... You must not live? All kinds of people live in this wide world—are you alone not to live? The one made of baseness—the one of deceitful character—the one who breaks integrity—the one who breaks affection—the arrogant man lives too, my beauty! Are you alone not to live? The blood-mad man who raves ‘war, war’ lives too, my painted doll! Are you alone not to live? My treasure! In this world the treacherous man whose belly burns at seeing others live also lives—the heartless cruel man also lives—my diamond full moon! Are you alone not to live? The man who says one person must labour and another must flourish, while he himself came by without labour, lives happily too, Anjugame! Who said you must not live?... My life! Maykkainatha Swami, the silk-pitambara mendicant who deceives the town saying, ‘I am the Lord who performs the tandava—therefore fill this alms bowl,’ lives too—with drums and clamour and a thousand flag-bearers!
notes: The source's accumulating political and religious satire is preserved rather than softened.
`அஞ்சுகமே` is retained as the affectionate vocative `Anjugame` rather than assigned an unsupported modern gloss.
`தாண்டவம்` is retained as `tandava`; the mocked alms-bowl claim is translated only as printed.

source_locator.description: The verified derivative records that Muthan's preceding PDF 104 speech continues unlabelled on PDF 105 before Muthayi speaks.

translation.english_text: Those snakes may live, tender vine! Why should you not live?... The Vengai ruler—the megalomaniac who turned beautiful Tirunagar into Pazhuthar, plundered its gold and goods and, not satisfied with that, enslaved the very soil—lives with his henchmen and immense influence! Tribute-payers—kavadi-bearers—heralds—those who make a living washing feet—all live happily, beautiful-eyed one, on this earth!... Moon-lotus! Who said that you alone must not live?
notes: The source prints no new speaker label at the PDF 104→105 continuation. Muthan attribution remains `source-context-attributed` derivative provenance and is not manufactured as a printed label.

The supplement is represented separately because the closed source-role layer already owns this unlabelled continuation; it is not retroactively merged into the immutable explicit record `ammaiyappan-s059-d008`.

translation.english_text: Can a deer live in a tiger forest, Aththan?...

Honour is sharper than a tiger's claw, flower-vine! Songbirds that sing in the forest must live among eagles and vultures, my love! After I am gone, you too must live among this crowd of people without virtue. You must live not for yourself, but for the treasure of our love growing in your womb—the child, the fruit of nectar—the speaking golden picture. Even if I cannot see it, you are the one who will behold and rejoice in it; you are the one who must protect it!... My life, that child of joy is the one who will proclaim loudly into the ear of this world that Muthan's lineage has not been wiped out root and branch! Thinking of that future, even now I let out a sigh of happiness...
notes: The deer/tiger and songbird/predator imagery is preserved as source rhetoric.
The unborn child is described through the source's accumulating metaphors; English does not add biological or narrative detail beyond the printed speech.

translation.english_text: Aththan....
Do not cry, my dear! Do not cry! Let me see you once with a smiling face, so my heart may be cooled. Come, my Senthamizh! Show me a smile...
notes: `செந்தமிழே` is retained as the affectionate poetic vocative `Senthamizh` rather than flattened into an ordinary pet name.

translation.english_text: Aththan...

I kissed your honey-dripping lips. The world did not like it—justice, fairness—so now I am going to kiss honour! One last thing I ask, Muthayi; one last thing I ask! That love song the two of us used to sing together—where will I ever hear it again? Come, sing it once!... Sing, my dear! If you do not sing, your lover will not die in peace... Sing, my dear, sing!
notes: The source's compressed `உலகுக்கு நீதிக்கு—நியாயத்துக்கு—` sequence is rendered from its immediate rhetorical contrast without changing the frozen Tamil.

This immutable dialogue owns the source-visible request for `that love song we used to sing together` and is linked to `ammaiyappan-song-005`. The booklet prints no title, lyric body or authorship, and none is reconstructed.

source_locator.description: Muthayi sings through her tears while Muthan walks toward the gallows; no song title or lyric body is printed.

translation.english_text: [She sings through her tears. He keeps walking toward the gallows.]
notes: This unit owns only the distinct source-visible performance cue. The preceding labelled Muthan dialogue separately owns the request and links the same occurrence ID.

The booklet prints no title, lyric lines or authorship for this performance. The archive does not merge this unnamed occurrence with another unnamed love-song identity without stronger source evidence.

source_locator.description: The Vengaiyur king and Poongavanam are nearby while Boopathi speaks looking at a golden lotus.

translation.english_text: [The king of Vengaiyur is there, with Poongavanam nearby. Physician Boopathi speaks while looking at a lotus made of gold.]

A beautiful lotus flower—the sculptor has made it wonderfully... Its golden petals glitter as though they would seize the eye.... Yet this flower has no fragrance, Maharaja!... That is what Princess Poongavanam's life has become!...
Maharaja!... After Physician Boopathi has told you so much, do you now understand why I refused to marry you?
I understand, Poongavanam! If you had revealed this reason earlier, how much more peaceful my life would have been!
Maharaja! Forgive me. I have done you a great wrong. Not only to you; I have wronged womankind itself! Maharaja, somehow set my son free!
Poongavanam! For the love I bore you alone, I could release Muthan. But Muthan is an enemy of Vengai Nadu!... a seeker of freedom!... There is no law by which I can release him......
notes: `விடுதலை விரும்பி` is preserved as `seeker of freedom`, retaining the source's political charge rather than reducing it to a generic offender label.

translation.english_text: Maharaja!... Must Muthan die?... Must my son die?... Then kill me too...
Do not grieve! Muthan is being released because he is the son of the woman who has lived in my heart all this time!...

source_locator.description: Muthan is taken toward the gallows through a large crowd; his friends create a diversion, remove him, and soldiers take a black-masked prisoner onward believing him to be Muthan.

translation.english_text: [Muthan is being taken to the gallows... A huge crowd. Muthan's friends are among them. Maappillaithaasu Swamigal, Baladevar and Sukhadev are also there. Muthan's friends communicate by signs.... Suddenly confusion breaks out in the crowd. Muthan's friends take Muthan away. The confusion subsides. The soldiers, mistaking a black-masked prisoner for Muthan, drag him toward the gallows.]
notes: The source presents the rescue and mistaken-prisoner substitution entirely as stage action; English does not invent dialogue or identify the masked prisoner before the next scene reveals him.

source_locator.description: As the masked figure is being hanged, the rope is cut and Poongavanam runs in.

translation.english_text: [As the masked figure is being hanged, the rope is cut. Poongavanam runs in.]
Muthaa!... Muthaa!...

source_locator.description: Poongavanam removes the cloth covering the face, sees Maappillaithaasar, and cries out.

translation.english_text: [She removes the cloth covering the face. Maappillaithaasar is revealed there.... She cries out.]
What is this? The swami instead of Muthan?... How did this happen?...

Elder!... I will tell you! I know how the swami got changed!... Muthan's friends freed Muthan, stripped off his black clothes, threw them away and ran... Seeing that, the swami immediately put on those clothes himself and stood like Muthan... These soldiers were deceived and, thinking the swami was Muthan—like this—this way—it happened.
notes: The source's deliberately halting ending `இப்படி—இது மாதிரி—நடந்து விட்டது` is preserved rather than smoothed into a more procedural explanation.

translation.english_text: No one need be surprised! This is the end I sought for myself. I have made atonement for my crimes. This is the first and last sacrifice I make for my son! On the earth where Pattinathar, the eighteen Siddhars, and virtuous ascetics lived, I came as a stain; here, I perish! Poongavanam! Poongavanam! Forgive me! Forgive me! All of you, forgive me! Forgive me!...
notes: The Pattinathar / eighteen-Siddhars sequence is translated only as printed; no external religious biography or attribution is added.

source_locator.description: The swami's speech ends and his life ends.

translation.english_text: [The speech ends; the swami's life ends.]
notes: The source's parallel phrasing `பேச்சு முடிகிறது; சாமியாரின் வாழ்க்கை முடிகிறது` is retained rather than expanded into additional death action.

source_locator.description: Muthayi lies fallen; Muthan and his comrades arrive.

translation.english_text: [Muthayi lies fallen. Muthan and his comrades arrive.]
Muthayi! Muthayi!...
Aththan!...
notes: `அத்தான்` is retained as `Aththan`, consistent with the established lover/kinship register.

translation.english_text: My jewel!...

source_locator.description: Poongavanam, Baladevar, Boopathi and Sukhadev arrive.

translation.english_text: [Poongavanam, Baladevar, Boopathi and Sukhadev arrive.]
Muthaa...
Princess...
Muthaa!... The princess is your mother!... The mother who gave birth to you!...
Ah...
Yes, Aththan! She is your mother!
My mother?.... Amma!... How wrongly I thought of you in every way—forgive me, Amma! Forgive me!...
notes: `அம்மா` is retained as `Amma` in the recognition scene to preserve the sudden intimate shift from `Princess` to mother-address.

translation.english_text: Muthaa!...

Muthaa!... Love and motherhood have won!... Now you must win in duty!... Karmaveeran, raised together with tears! You are the commander worthy of fighting for the liberation of the motherland!... Muthayi, you and your husband must labour for the liberation of Pazhuthar... Luxury in the grove, in the breeze! Then—swing the sword to defend your own country!
notes: `கர்ம வீரனே` is retained as `Karmaveeran` rather than assigned a doctrinal gloss unsupported by the immediate source.
The closing imperative preserves the source's turn from private love/family reunion toward Pazhuthar and motherland liberation.

translation.english_text:
I know, sir!

In love, in its ripening,
the talk is of going to battle!...
For husband and wife,
the motherland itself is breath!...

Dear comrades! Beloved younger brothers!... Everyone, set out!... Let us break Annal's shackles! Let us redeem Pazhuthar! Come! He who has a younger brother fears no army! If this army is defeated, what army can win!... Come! Come!
notes: The four-line stanza remains inside immutable dialogue record `ammaiyappan-s063-d012`; the closed song/performance inventory authorizes no separate song or literary-verse occurrence in scene 63.

Frozen `அண்ணலின் விலங்கொடிப்ப ோம்` is rendered with `Annal` retained as a transliterated source term because the immediate referent is not secure enough for a stronger English gloss; no Tamil normalization is claimed.
The compact martial saying `தம்பி உடையான்படைக்கஞ்சான்! இப்படை தோற்கின் எப்படை ஜெயிக்கும்!` is translated as printed rhetoric rather than replaced by an external proverb text.
